item.title: Daily: stocks Risk On, Bitcoin Balanced
item.description: No trade. Neither desk changed state, so the portfolio holds as it is.

item.title: Weekly note: The index held. What sits underneath it did not.
item.description: US stocks had their worst week since early June, driven by a two-day unwind of the AI and semiconductor trade, and neither desk changed its call. The stocks desk is still Risk On at 100% invested, the Bitcoin desk still Balanced at 50%, and the flagship is still 85% invested. That is not the models shrugging. The stocks composite score fell from +0.086 to +0.03 over the week, its weakest reading in months, and the price that would cut equity exposure in half moved up to about $726 from $722. The call did not change; the distance to the next call shrank to roughly 1%. The more useful fact is why the score is still positive at all. Of the +0.03 total, the calendar group contributes +0.048 on its own, from November seasonality and the second year of the presidential cycle. Strip the calendar out and the composite is roughly -0.018. The only group holding the score above water is the one with the smallest weight and the shortest shelf life, and it fades mechanically as November ends. For the call to stay where it is past the turn of the month, something in trend or internals has to improve. Market internals are the single largest drag, at -0.09 of the composite, and their shape matters more than their size. Semiconductors are down 14.3% against the S&P over three months, a reading all but pinned at the model's floor. Consumer discretionary is down 7.3% against staples, high yield is down 1.9% against Treasuries, and emerging markets are down 4.3% against the S&P. But the equal-weight S&P is up 3.1% against the cap-weighted index. Those two facts together do not describe broad risk aversion, which would show up as the average stock lagging the index, not beating it. They describe a concentrated unwind of the market's leadership with a defensive rotation underneath it. The median stock is weathering this better than the index is. Friday's jobs report is the week's most under-appreciated development, because it cuts the opposite way to how it reads. Payrolls rose 165,000 against expectations near 65,000, unemployment fell to 4.1%, and August and September were revised up by a combined 84,000. On an ordinary week that is good news. This week it pushed market-implied odds of a Federal Reserve rate increase at the December meeting to 78% from 70%, and lifted the two-year yield six basis points. Two of the five risk conditions the stocks desk currently flags are rate-driven: the three-month bill is up 0.44 points in six months and the ten-year is up 0.81 points. A strong labour market now feeds the tightening side of the model rather than the growth side. For the next few months, strong data is a headwind for this portfolio's equity sleeve, not a tailwind, and that is an awkward position for a long-only investor to sit in. Fear rose but did not reach an extreme. The VIX closed at 25.6, up about 80% from its three-month low of 14.2, and realized volatility is 19.9% annualized. Even so, the model's volatility capitulation factor still reads zero: by its standard this is elevated stress, not panic, and panic is usually what marks a tradeable low. Consumer sentiment is a separate oddity worth knowing about. At 48.1 it is depressed enough that the model counts it as a contrarian positive, one of the few inputs actively helping the score. Weak sentiment alongside a strong labour market is an unusual pairing, and it is part of why the composite has held up better than the tape. All three of the desk's experimental confirmation signals are on at once: fewer than 60% of major risk assets above their 200-day average, now 33% of nine, a 44-point fall in that share over three months, and high yield against Treasuries in its worst quintile. In the study behind them, that configuration accompanied the seven declines of 10% or more from a running high since 2006. These deserve a heavy caveat and we will keep repeating it: they were chosen from 21 candidates tested against 24 warning episodes, which is far more tests than events, they remain unvalidated on forward data, and they change no exposure whatsoever. Treat them as a flag to watch, not as evidence. The concrete line to know is this. If SPY were to close near $726 and hold there for five sessions with every other input unchanged, the stocks desk would move to Balanced and the flagship would go from 85% invested to roughly 55%, with cash rising from 15% to about 45%. The five-session hold matters: a single bad print does not do it, which is the model's deliberate slowness. Two pieces of options context sit on top of that level. The heaviest SPY put open interest is at the 725 strike, essentially on the model's own trigger, and estimated dealer gamma was negative across the entire range we checked at the Nov 5 close. Negative gamma means hedging flows tend to amplify moves rather than cushion them. None of that changes a call, and dealer positioning is an estimate resting on an assumption that is often wrong. But it is a reason to expect that if that zone is reached, it may be reached quickly. Bitcoin's setup is asymmetric and the constraint is not Bitcoin. The desk sits at 50% invested and needs roughly 11.7%, a move to about $84,800, before it would go fully invested; its score is +0.07 against a +0.20 threshold. The largest single negative input is not price or momentum but the dollar, with the dollar proxy up 3.2% over three months. Bitcoin's route back to a full position runs through the currency more than through its own chart. One nuance cuts against the easy read of Thursday's session, when Bitcoin fell alongside the Nasdaq and looked like levered technology exposure. Over the last 13 weeks its correlation to the S&P 500 is -0.29 while its correlation to gold is +0.54. This quarter it has behaved more like a monetary hedge than a technology proxy, and a single correlated down-day does not overturn that. What is ahead: October CPI on Tuesday Nov 10 at 8:30 a.m. ET, producer prices on Friday Nov 13, and the Federal Reserve decision on Wednesday Dec 9. CPI is the input that matters most here, both because the inflation reading gates one of the desk's re-entry rules and because the December rate debate now turns on it. On our own record, the flagship is down 3.58% since inception against the S&P 500's 3.47%, over ten sessions. Ten sessions is too short to judge, and we will keep saying so until the count passes 60. Nothing here is investment advice, and the model portfolio is hypothetical.
